hints.content:
A figure has **rotational symmetry** if there is a rotation that maps the figure onto itself.

Any line segment in the figure would have to map onto a congruent line segment in the same figure.  

Further, the segment lengths and angles between them must repeat in the same order around the center.

The **magnitude** of the rotation is the number of degrees we can rotate the figure to map it onto itself.

Will the parallelogram map onto itself with $180\degree$ and $270\degree$ rotations about the origin?

Let's check the rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin.

The figure maps onto itself, so it is **symmetric** about the origin at a $180\degree$ magnitude of rotation.



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A parallelogram mapped onto a coordinate plane. The x- y-coordinate plane scales by ones. The center of the parallelogram is at the origin. The parallelogram has a point at negative seven, negative one, a point at negative three, negative five, a point at three, five, and a point at seven, one. An arc shows the pre-image was rotated one hundred eighty degrees to form the image mapped onto the pre-image.

hints.content:
Let's check the rotation of $270^\circ$ about the origin.

Some points on the parallelogram map to points which are not on the figure. So the parallelogram does **not** have rotational symmetry at a magnitude of $270^\circ$.



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A parallelogram mapped onto a coordinate plane. The x- y-coordinate plane scales by ones. The center of the parallelogram is at the origin. The parallelogram has a point at negative seven, negative one, a point at negative three, negative five, a point at three, five, and a point at seven, one. An arc shows the pre-image was rotated two hundred seventy degrees to form an image not mapped onto the pre-image.

hints.content:
This is the completed table:

Rotation | Applies to the figure?
:- | :-:
Rotational symmetry of $180^\circ$ about the origin | Yes
Rotational symmetry of $270^\circ$ about the origin | No
